options.text: Lipid molecules that store energy
Biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions
Nucleic acids that carry genetic information
Carbohydrate molecules that provide structure

questions.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts, usually proteins, that speed up chemical reactions in living organisms without being used up in the process.

questions.stem: What is the active site of an enzyme?

options.text: The amino acid chain before it folds
A specific region on the enzyme where the substrate binds
The part of the enzyme that is denatured
The entire surface of the enzyme

questions.explanation: The active site is a specific region on the enzyme molecule with a precise shape that is complementary to the shape of the substrate, allowing the substrate to bind.

questions.stem: What is the lock and key model of enzyme action?

options.text: Enzymes lock onto cells to destroy them
Substrates are locked inside the enzyme permanently
Enzymes change shape to fit any substrate
The substrate has a complementary shape to the active site, fitting together like a lock and key

questions.explanation: The lock and key model proposes that the substrate fits precisely into the active site of the enzyme, like a key fitting into a lock, because their shapes are complementary.

questions.stem: Why does increasing temperature initially increase enzyme activity?

options.text: The enzyme changes shape
The active site gets larger
Substrate molecules have more kinetic energy, increasing the frequency of successful collisions with the active site
More enzymes are produced

questions.explanation: Higher temperatures give both enzyme and substrate molecules more kinetic energy, leading to more frequent collisions and more enzyme-substrate complexes forming per unit time.

questions.stem: What happens to an enzyme above its optimum temperature?

options.text: Nothing changes
It works even faster
It becomes denatured as bonds holding its shape break
It produces more substrate

questions.explanation: Above the optimum temperature, the bonds maintaining the enzyme's 3D shape begin to break, causing the active site to change shape (denaturation). The substrate can no longer fit.

questions.stem: Why are enzymes described as specific?

options.text: They work at any temperature
They can break down any substance
They are found in all cells
Each enzyme can only catalyse one type of reaction because only one substrate fits its active site

questions.explanation: Enzymes are specific because the shape of the active site is complementary to only one substrate (or a small group of similar substrates), so each enzyme catalyses only one type of reaction.

questions.stem: What is meant by the optimum pH of an enzyme?

options.text: The pH at which the enzyme works most efficiently
The pH at which the enzyme is produced
The pH at which the enzyme is destroyed
The pH of water

questions.explanation: The optimum pH is the pH value at which an enzyme works at its maximum rate. Different enzymes have different optimum pH values; for example, pepsin works best at pH 2 in the stomach.
